sections.heading: An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone and can outlive its instance

plan.problem: A server needs a disk that keeps its data when the server stops or breaks. An EBS volume is that disk, but it does not sit inside the server.
trace: **Create the volume.** An EBS volume is a [durable, block-level storage device] that you use [as you would use a physical hard drive] (ebs-volume-block-storage-device-like-hard-drive); it arrives as [raw, unformatted block devices], so you create a file system first (ebs-volume-raw-unformatted-block-device).
**Attach it in the same zone.** You can [attach multiple EBS volumes to a single instance], but the volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone] (ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance).

**Writes are copied inside the zone.** The volume is [automatically replicated within its Availability Zone], which protects against the [failure of any single hardware component] (ebs-volume-replicated-within-az).

**The volume outlives the instance.** It is [off-instance storage] that can [persist independently from the running life] of the instance (ebs-volume-persists-independently-of-instance), and it [remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle] (ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start).

**Termination decides per volume.** The root volume created at launch is [deleted when that instance is terminated] (ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true); other volumes created at launch [are not deleted when that instance is terminated] (ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false).
plan.table: What happens to each volume (columns: Event | Root volume created at launch | Other EBS volume): reboot | kept | kept; stop and start | kept | kept (ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start); terminate, default flag | deleted (ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true) | kept (ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false); terminate, flag changed at launch | kept with [DeleteOnTermination to false] (ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true) | deleted with [DeleteOnTermination to true] (ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false).
plan.why: Why keep the data off the instance? The instance can fail or be replaced, while the data must stay; that is also why you keep paying for a volume [as long as the data persists] (ebs-volume-charged-while-data-persists), until you delete it. The EC2 best practices keep [separate Amazon EBS volumes for the operating system] and for data (ec2-bp-separate-ebs-for-os-and-data).
plan.exam_signal: "the data must stay after the instance is terminated" points to the [Delete on termination flag] of the root volume (ebs-faq-root-delete-on-termination-no); "use the data in another Availability Zone" points to a snapshot and a new volume, which can [create a duplicate volume in that zone] (ebs-snapshot-restore-volume-other-az).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: to detach a running data volume [you must first unmount the volume], or the data [might be out of sync] (ebs-detach-running-instance-unmount-first); a root volume needs a stop first ([you must stop the instance], ebs-detach-root-volume-stop-instance). Device names on Nitro instances (ebs-nvme-devices-on-nitro) and latency (ebs-faq-average-latency) are reference only here.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a volume is block storage that stays in one zone. The thing to watch is the delete flag on the root volume.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team terminates an instance that was launched with a root volume and a second data volume, both with default settings. Which volume still exists? Answer: the data volume; the root volume is [deleted when that instance is terminated] (ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true), and other volumes created at launch [are not deleted when that instance is terminated] (ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false).

sections.heading: Instance store data lives on the host and ends with the instance

plan.problem: Some data is needed only while a job runs: a cache, a buffer, scratch files. It must be fast, and it can disappear.
trace: **Disks on the host.** Instance store is [temporary block-level storage] on disks [physically attached to the host computer] (instance-store-physically-attached-host-disks).

**Chosen with the type.** Its size [varies by instance type and instance size], and [not every instance type provides instance store volumes] (instance-store-size-varies-by-type); the letter d in a type name means [Instance store volumes] (ec2-instance-type-option-letters). You add it [only when you launch it] (instance-store-attach-only-at-launch), and [There is no additional charge] (instance-store-no-additional-charge).
**Fast.** SSD instance store gives [high random I/O performance with very low latency] (instance-store-ssd-high-random-io).

**Gone after a stop.** Data [persists even if the instance is rebooted], but not when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated] (instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), and not when [The underlying disk fails] (instance-store-data-lost-when-disk-fails).
**Tied to its instance.** [You can’t detach an instance store volume] and attach it elsewhere (instance-store-tied-to-instance-lifetime); copy the display with its curly apostrophe.
plan.table: Where the data survives (columns: Event | Instance store | EBS volume): reboot | kept | kept; stop or hibernate | erased (instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop) | kept (ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start); disk failure | lost (instance-store-data-lost-when-disk-fails) | replicated in its zone (ebs-volume-replicated-within-az); in an AMI or snapshot | [not included in the EBS-backed AMI] (instance-store-data-not-in-ebs-backed-ami) | snapshots.
plan.why: Why does a stop erase it? The disks belong to the host computer, and a started instance is [moved to a new host computer] (ec2-stop-start-moves-host-loses-instance-store).
plan.exam_signal: "temporary data", "cache", "buffers" or "scratch data" with the fastest local I/O points to instance store ([buffers, caches, scratch data], instance-store-ideal-for-temporary-data); "the data must survive a stop" points to an EBS volume.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence each: AWS recommends instance store [only for temporary data] (instance-store-faq-only-temporary-data); NVMe instance store is encrypted with an [XTS-AES-256 block cipher] (instance-store-nvme-encryption-xts-aes-256; subsection 12 can use this instead). Reference only: first-write initialization, the 10 percent unpartitioned advice, r8id sizes, instance store root volumes (end of life, ec2-s3-backed-ami-end-of-life).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: instance store is fast scratch space on the host. The thing to watch is a stop, which erases it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team caches thumbnails on instance store and stops the instance every night to save money. What do they find each morning? Answer: an empty cache; the data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated] (instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop). A reboot would have kept it.

sections.heading: SSD volumes serve small random I/O, and HDD volumes serve large sequential reads

plan.problem: A database reads and writes many small pieces in random places. A log job reads huge files from start to end. One kind of disk is not the cheapest for both.
trace: **Two families.** EBS has [SSD-backed storage for transactional workloads] and [HDD-backed storage for throughput intensive workloads] (ebs-ssd-transactional-hdd-throughput-categories).
**SSD counts operations.** SSD volumes suit [transactional, IOPS-intensive database workloads, boot volumes] (ebs-faq-ssd-workloads).

**HDD counts megabytes.** st1 and sc1 are [low-cost magnetic storage] that measures performance [in terms of throughput rather than IOPS] (ebs-hdd-performance-in-throughput-not-iops), built for [large, sequential I/O] (ebs-hdd-large-sequential-not-small-random).

**Pick the HDD by scan rate.** st1 serves [frequently accessed, throughput-intensive workloads] (ebs-st1-low-cost-frequent-throughput); sc1 has [the lowest cost per GB] for [less frequently accessed workloads] (ebs-sc1-lowest-cost-per-gb).
plan.table: Volume types at a glance (columns: Type | Family | Built for | Boot volume?): gp3 | SSD | [medium sized single instance databases], [boot volumes] (ebs-gp3-use-cases) | yes; io2 Block Express | SSD | [I/O-intensive NoSQL & relational databases] (ebs-io2-use-cases) | yes (SSD: ebs-faq-ssd-workloads); st1 | HDD | [Big data, data warehouses, log processing] (ebs-st1-use-cases) | no ([Bootable st1 volumes are not supported], ebs-hdd-volumes-not-bootable); sc1 | HDD | [Colder data requiring fewer scans per day] (ebs-sc1-use-cases) | no ([Bootable sc1 volumes are not supported]).
plan.why: Why do small random reads fail on HDD? An HDD I/O of [1 MiB or less counts as a 1 MiB I/O credit] (ebs-hdd-io-counted-as-1-mib), so many small reads use up the volume quickly; a database [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes] (ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io).
plan.exam_signal: "big data", "log processing", "data warehouse" or "throughput-intensive, sequential" points to st1 ([Big data, data warehouses, log processing], ebs-st1-use-cases); "cold data", "infrequently accessed" with the lowest cost points to sc1 ([the lowest cost per GB], ebs-sc1-lowest-cost-per-gb).
plan.diagram: ebs-volume-ladder, after the table (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: io size caps (ebs-io-size-cap-ssd-hdd), merging (ebs-io-merge-and-split), st1 and sc1 maxima (B-list), Magnetic volumes as [previous generation volumes] (ebs-magnetic-standard-is-previous-generation; one clause at most), and that a root volume [can't be modified to an st1 or sc1 volume] (ebs-root-volume-cannot-change-to-hdd; subsection 7 uses it).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: SSD for many small random reads, HDD for long sequential scans. The thing to watch is the boot volume: keep it on SSD.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team keeps 10 TB of logs that one job scans once a week. It wants the lowest-cost block storage. st1 or sc1? Answer: sc1, for [Colder data requiring fewer scans per day] (ebs-sc1-use-cases) at [the lowest cost per GB] (ebs-sc1-lowest-cost-per-gb); st1 fits work that needs scans of [up to 500 MiB/s] or several full scans a day (ebs-st1-vs-sc1-scan-choice). The 10 TB and the weekly scan are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: gp3 lets you buy IOPS and throughput without buying more storage

plan.problem: A small database needs high IOPS but little space. With gp2 you buy space to get speed; with gp3 you buy each one on its own.
trace: **Start at the baseline.** Every gp3 volume gets [3,000 IOPS] (ebs-gp3-baseline-iops) and [125 MiB/s] (ebs-gp3-baseline-throughput) at any size, in the storage price; gp3 does not burst, it keeps that level (ebs-faq-gp3-no-burst).

**Add performance on its own.** You raise IOPS and throughput [independently of volume size] (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), up to [80,000] IOPS at [500 IOPS per GiB] (ebs-gp3-max-iops-80000) and [2,000 MiB/s] (ebs-gp3-max-throughput-2000); the extra is charged in [IOPS per month and MB/s per month] (ebs-pricing-gp3-iops-throughput-billed-separately).
**Compare gp2.** gp2 baseline IOPS grow at [3 IOPS per GiB] of size (ebs-gp2-iops-per-gib); a gp2 volume [smaller than 1 TiB] can [burst to 3,000 IOPS] on I/O credits (ebs-gp2-burst-3000-iops).
**Pay less per GiB.** gp3 has a [20 percent lower price per GiB] than gp2 (ebs-gp3-20-percent-lower-price) and is [the lowest cost SSD volume] (ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd).
plan.table: gp3 or gp2 (columns: Question | gp3 | gp2): baseline IOPS | [3,000 IOPS] at every size | [3 IOPS per GiB]; more IOPS | provision them | grow the volume ([performance scales with volume size], ebs-gp2-performance-scales-with-size); burst | none, a constant baseline (ebs-faq-gp3-no-burst) | [burst to 3,000 IOPS] below 1 TiB; price per GiB | [20 percent lower price per GiB] | higher.
plan.why: Why separate size and speed? They are two different needs; gp3 lets you provision performance [without needing to provision additional block storage capacity] (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), and you pay for what you provision (ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month).
plan.exam_signal: "cost-effective" with "boot volumes", "development and test" or "medium-sized databases" points to gp3 ([balance between cost and performance], ebs-faq-gp3-suited-workloads); "more IOPS, no more storage" points to gp3 with provisioned IOPS (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: gp2 credits and the move to gp3. A gp2 volume earns [3 I/O credits per GiB of volume size per second] (ebs-gp2-credit-earn-rate), starts with an [initial I/O credit balance of 5.4 million I/O credits] (ebs-gp2-initial-credit-balance) and holds at most [5.4 million I/O credits] (ebs-gp2-credit-accrual-limit). A gp2 volume of [5,334 GiB and larger] has the gp2 maximum IOPS (ebs-gp2-max-iops-size). A change from gp2 to gp3 with no IOPS given keeps at least the gp2 performance (ebs-modify-gp2-to-gp3-auto-performance, guide example; link only if a display reads cleanly). At most 75 words.
plan.body_extras: Do not state the gp3 maximums as the reason in an Exam signal or a Stop and answer: they changed on 2025-09-26 (Changed recently in 1-fast.md). One clause may say that older questions use the earlier [16,000 IOPS] (ebs-gp3-max-iops-80000). The console default (ebs-gp3-console-default-type) and per-second billing (ebs-billing-per-second-60-second-minimum) are reference only.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: gp3 sells space, IOPS and throughput separately. The thing to watch is gp2, where more speed means a bigger volume.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team runs a 200 GiB gp2 volume that gives too few IOPS to its database. The team does not need more space. What is the cheapest fix? Answer: change it to gp3 and provision the IOPS; gp3 performance scales [independently of volume size] (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size) at a [20 percent lower price per GiB] (ebs-gp3-20-percent-lower-price). The 200 GiB is an example value in the prompt.

sections.heading: io2 Block Express buys more IOPS, lower latency and higher durability

plan.problem: Some databases need more than gp3 gives: more IOPS on one volume, latency below a millisecond, or a smaller chance of losing the volume. That costs more, so a requirement must ask for it.
trace: **Know where gp3 ends.** AWS recommends io2 Block Express for [higher durability, better latency consistency] or more IOPS and throughput than gp3 (ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when).
**Provision the IOPS.** One io2 Block Express volume takes [up to 256,000] IOPS at [1,000:1] IOPS per GiB (ebs-io2-max-iops-ratio) and [up to 4,000 MiB/s] (ebs-io2-max-throughput).
**Lower latency.** Average EBS latency is [single-digit milliseconds]; for io2 Block Express it is [sub-millisecond] (ebs-faq-average-latency).
**Higher durability.** io2 Block Express is designed for [99.999 percent volume durability] (ebs-io2-durability-afr); gp3 for [99.8 percent to 99.9 percent] (ebs-gp3-durability-afr).
**Use a Nitro instance.** Other instance types reach [up to 32,000 IOPS] (ebs-io2-nitro-iops-limit).
plan.table: gp3 or io2 Block Express (columns: Question | gp3 | io2 Block Express): IOPS per volume | [80,000] at most (ebs-gp3-max-iops-80000) | [up to 256,000] (ebs-io2-max-iops-ratio); latency | [single-digit millisecond latency] (ebs-gp3-latency) | [sub-millisecond] (ebs-faq-average-latency); durability | [99.8 percent to 99.9 percent] | [99.999 percent volume durability]; delivers its performance | [99 percent of the time] (ebs-gp3-performance-99-percent) | [99.9 percent of the time] (ebs-piops-99-9-percent); Multi-Attach | no | yes, io1 and io2 [supported exclusively on] them (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only).
plan.why: Why pay more? io2 Block Express runs on the [next generation of Amazon EBS storage server architecture] (ebs-faq-block-express-definition), and its IOPS charges are tiered, so it is [more economical to scale IOPS] on one volume (ebs-pricing-io2-iops-tiered).
plan.exam_signal: "sub-millisecond latency", "I/O-intensive database" or "more IOPS than gp3 supports" points to io2 Block Express ([consistent sub-millisecond latency], ebs-io2-use-cases).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: io1, I/O size and billing. io1 runs from [4 GiB to 16 TiB] with [up to 64,000 IOPS per volume] (ebs-io1-size-and-iops-range) at [50:1] (ebs-io1-iops-ratio). Provisioned IOPS assume a base I/O size of [16KB] (ebs-faq-piops-base-io-size-16kb); with 256 KB I/Os an io2 volume reaches [16,000 IOPS], because it already moves [4000 MiB/s] (ebs-faq-io2-256kb-io-16000-iops). Provisioned IOPS are [billed for the IOPS provisioned] also while the volume is detached (ebs-faq-piops-billed-when-detached). At most 75 words.
plan.body_extras: Write 'io2 Block Express' for every io2 volume: since [April 30, 2025] every io2 volume is [io2 Block Express] (ebs-change-io2-all-block-express-2025-04). Reference only: under-500-microsecond latency, outlier latency, size range, tier prices.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: io2 Block Express is for the database that outgrows gp3. The thing to watch is the price of every provisioned IOPS.
plan.stop_and_answer: A database volume is io2 Block Express with 100,000 provisioned IOPS, but the instance type is not built on Nitro. What does the database get? Answer: the volume reaches [up to 32,000 IOPS] on that instance (ebs-io2-nitro-iops-limit); move to a Nitro-based type to use the provisioned IOPS. The 100,000 is an example value in the prompt.

sections.heading: The instance and its EBS bandwidth can cap a fast volume

plan.problem: A team provisions a fast volume, and the database is still slow. The volume is not the only limit on the path.
trace: **The smaller limit wins.** An instance's EBS performance is [bounded by the instance type's performance limits] or by its volumes, [whichever is smaller] (ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller).

**EBS-optimized bandwidth.** EBS-optimized instances give [dedicated bandwidth for Amazon EBS I/O] (ebs-optimized-dedicated-bandwidth); for current generation types it is [enabled by default at no additional cost] (ec2-ebs-optimized-default-current-generation).

**Stripe for more.** [Creating a RAID 0 array] gives a [higher level of performance for a file system] than one volume (ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume), but losing one volume means [complete data loss for the array] (ebs-raid0-one-volume-loss-loses-array).

**Or use one stronger volume.** For higher needs AWS recommends io2 Block Express volumes, [without needing the operational management of striping] (ebs-faq-stripe-prefer-io2; display requested as fr-0072: until it is filled, write the sentence with a <!-- needs-display --> marker, never with the 'We recommend' display).
plan.table: RAID on EBS (columns: Level | Effect | AWS advice): RAID 0 | adds the IOPS and throughput of each volume | use it when one volume is not enough (ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume); RAID 1 | writes every block twice | [RAID 1 is also not recommended] (ebs-raid1-not-recommended); RAID 5 and RAID 6 | [parity write operations] use IOPS | [RAID 5 and RAID 6 are not recommended] (ebs-raid5-raid6-not-recommended).
plan.why: Why does the instance matter? Every I/O leaves the instance for off-instance storage, and EBS is a [multi-tenant block storage service] that uses [rate limiting] (ebs-faq-multi-tenant-rate-limiting).
plan.exam_signal: "the volume never reaches its provisioned IOPS" points to the instance's EBS limit ([whichever is smaller], ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller); "more performance than one volume" points to RAID 0 ([Creating a RAID 0 array], ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume) or io2 Block Express (ebs-faq-stripe-prefer-io2).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug prompt: a team builds a RAID 5 array from four gp3 volumes to get speed and protection against a volume failure. What is wrong? Reveal: AWS says [RAID 5 and RAID 6 are not recommended], because their [parity write operations] use IOPS (ebs-raid5-raid6-not-recommended); each volume is already [automatically replicated within its Availability Zone] (ebs-volume-replicated-within-az). Use RAID 0 or one io2 Block Express volume for speed, and snapshots for protection. About 60 words with the reveal.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeStalledIOCheck (ebs-metric-volume-iops-exceeded-check, ebs-metric-volume-stalled-io-check), free 1-minute metrics while attached (ebs-cloudwatch-metrics-free-only-when-attached), [arrays larger than 8 volumes] (ebs-raid-over-8-volumes-diminishing), the attachment limit that [depends on the instance type and instance size] (ec2-volume-attachment-limit-by-type-and-size). Do not state a per-instance volume count: the brief.v0 demand d039 stayed partial.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the instance has its own EBS limit. The thing to watch is RAID 0: one lost volume loses the array.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team attaches two io2 Block Express volumes of 40,000 IOPS each to an instance type whose EBS limit is lower than their sum. What limits the database? Answer: the instance; performance is bounded by the instance limits or the volumes, [whichever is smaller] (ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller). The IOPS values are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: Elastic Volumes grows or retunes a volume in place but cannot shrink it

plan.problem: A volume fills up at night, or a database needs more IOPS after a launch. Nobody wants to stop the server or copy the data to a new volume.
trace: **Modify in place.** Elastic Volumes can [increase the volume size, change the volume type] or adjust performance [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance] (ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).

**The size counts early.** A size increase works once the modification [reaches the optimizing state] (ebs-modification-size-effective-at-optimizing); the whole change can take [up to six hours] for a 1-TiB volume (ebs-modify-duration-1-tib).
**Grow the file system.** After a size increase [you must also extend the volume's partition] and file system (ebs-extend-partition-after-size-increase).
**Pay for the new setting.** [There is no charge to modify the configuration]; the new configuration is billed [after volume modification starts] (ebs-modification-free-charged-new-config).
**No way down.** [You can't decrease the volume size]; to shrink, you [create a smaller volume] and copy the data (ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease).
plan.table: What Elastic Volumes changes in place (columns: Change | In place?): larger size | yes, then extend the file system (ebs-extend-partition-after-size-increase); gp2 to gp3, more IOPS or throughput | yes (ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach); root volume to st1 or sc1 | no: it [can't be modified to an st1 or sc1 volume] (ebs-root-volume-cannot-change-to-hdd); smaller size | no (ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease).
plan.why: Why plan the size at all? You pay for the storage you provision, [charged by the amount of GB] each month (ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month), so start near the need and grow when the data grows.
plan.exam_signal: "increase storage or IOPS with no downtime" points to Elastic Volumes ([without detaching the volume or restarting the instance], ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: one volume can change [up to four times within a rolling 24-hour period] (ebs-elastic-volumes-four-modifications-24h), each after the previous one reaches [reach the `completed` state] (ebs-modify-wait-for-completed; use only if the display reads cleanly), and [You can't cancel a volume modification request] (ebs-modification-cannot-cancel). Do not write the old waiting rule: no saved page states it (register-22 for_writers). Reference only: MBR and GPT size limits (B-list candidate), Multi-Attach type changes.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: grow or retune a volume while it runs. The thing to watch is that a volume grows but does not shrink.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team grew a volume from 100 GiB to 300 GiB. The modification is in the optimizing state, but the operating system still shows 100 GiB. What is missing? Answer: extend the partition and the file system; after a size increase [you must also extend the volume's partition] (ebs-extend-partition-after-size-increase). The sizes are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: Multi-Attach shares one io2 volume, and the application must coordinate writes

plan.problem: A clustered database wants two servers to see the same disk, so that a standby can take over at once. A volume normally serves one instance.
trace: **Turn it on for io2.** Multi-Attach lets you [attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD] volume to several instances [in the same Availability Zone] (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az); it is [supported exclusively on] io1 and io2 (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only).

**Up to sixteen instances.** One volume attaches to [up to 16 instances] built on the Nitro System (ebs-multi-attach-16-nitro-instances), each with [full read and write permission] (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az).

**Coordinate the writes.** XFS and EXT4 are [not designed to be accessed simultaneously], so you [use a clustered file system] (ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), and [Your applications must provide write ordering] (ebs-multi-attach-io-fencing-write-ordering).
**Share the performance.** The [aggregate performance of all of the attached instances] [can't exceed the volume's maximum provisioned performance] (ebs-multi-attach-shares-provisioned-performance).
plan.table: Multi-Attach or Amazon EFS (columns: Question | Multi-Attach volume | Amazon EFS): what it is | one block volume | a [file storage service] (efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object); where clients run | one Availability Zone (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) | [within and across multiple Availability Zones] (ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing); what the application does | coordinates writes | reads and writes files; fits | clustered databases and failover | [shared read and write access across multiple Amazon EC2 instances] (ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access).
plan.why: Why the extra rules? Standard file systems are not built for several writers at once (ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), so safety comes from the application: [Windows Server Failover Cluster], [NVMe reservations] or an application that [coordinates safe access at the application-level] (ebs-faq-multi-attach-application-requirements).
plan.exam_signal: "shared block storage" for a "clustered application" in one Availability Zone points to io2 with Multi-Attach ([attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD], ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az); "shared files across Availability Zones" points to Amazon EFS (ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: Multi-Attach rules. A Multi-Attach volume [can't be created as boot volumes] (ebs-multi-attach-not-boot-volume). [Windows instances support Multi-Attach enabled io2 volumes only] (ebs-multi-attach-windows-io2-only). [You can't enable or disable Multi-Attach] while the volume is attached (ebs-multi-attach-toggle-only-when-detached). An issue in the EBS layer makes it [unavailable to all attached instances] (ebs-multi-attach-infrastructure-issue-all-instances). [There are no additional charges] for Multi-Attach itself (ebs-multi-attach-no-extra-charge). At most 75 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a cluster in one zone can share one io2 volume. The thing to watch is write safety from the cluster software.
plan.stop_and_answer: Twelve web servers in three Availability Zones need the same uploaded files. Is Multi-Attach the answer? Answer: no; Multi-Attach works [in the same Availability Zone] (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) and needs a clustered file system (ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system); Amazon EFS stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones] (ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing).

sections.heading: Each snapshot stores changed blocks but can restore the whole volume

plan.problem: Replication inside one zone does not bring back a deleted table, and it does not help when the zone is lost. A backup must live somewhere else and go back in time.
trace: **First a full copy, then changes.** Snapshots are [incremental backups]: after the first, EBS saves the [blocks on the volume that have changed] (ebs-snapshot-incremental-changed-blocks).

**Stored outside the zone.** The data is [stored redundantly in multiple Availability Zones] of Amazon S3 (ebs-snapshot-stored-in-s3-multiple-azs), in [S3 buckets that you can't access directly] (ebs-snapshot-s3-buckets-not-accessible).

**Keep working.** [Snapshot creation is asynchronous], and you [continue to use the volume during this time] (ebs-snapshot-async-volume-usable-while-pending); the snapshot [does not include data that has been cached] by the application (ebs-snapshot-excludes-cached-data).

**Delete old ones safely.** Deleting a snapshot removes [only the data that is referenced exclusively] by it (ebs-snapshot-delete-removes-only-exclusive-data), so you [retain only the most recent snapshot] to restore the volume (ebs-snapshot-deletion-keep-only-latest).
plan.table: What a snapshot holds and costs (columns: Question | Answer): what is saved | the changed blocks after the first snapshot (ebs-snapshot-incremental-changed-blocks); what you pay for | [the size of the data being backed up], [not the size of the source volume] (ebs-snapshot-charged-by-data-not-volume-size); how you reach it | the EC2 API, not the S3 API (ebs-faq-snapshots-not-via-s3-api); what deleting the volume does | [Deleting a volume has no effect] on its snapshots (ebs-snapshot-and-volume-delete-independent).
plan.why: Why is the backup your job? AWS [does not automatically back up the data]; [it is your responsibility to create EBS snapshots] (ebs-no-automatic-backup-customer-creates-snapshots). Saving changed blocks keeps each new snapshot small.
plan.exam_signal: "point-in-time backup of an EBS volume" points to a snapshot ([incremental backups], ebs-snapshot-incremental-changed-blocks); "a consistent backup of all volumes of an instance" points to multi-volume snapshots ([data coordinated, and crash-consistent snapshots], ebs-multi-volume-snapshots-crash-consistent).
plan.diagram: ebs-snapshot-chain, after the table (compare kind; caption and alt fixed in diagrams below).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: for a consistent snapshot AWS suggests you [pause writes to the volume] or unmount it (ebs-snapshot-consistency-pause-writes-or-unmount), and for a root volume to [stop the instance before taking the snapshot] (ebs-snapshot-root-volume-stop-instance-first). Reference only: AMI snapshots and deregistration (ebs-ami-*), VSS on Windows, the 16 TB FAQ (FAQ quick-fire uses it), HDD write slowdown during a snapshot.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a snapshot copies changed blocks to Amazon S3. The thing to watch is cached data that the application has not written yet.
plan.stop_and_answer: A volume has daily snapshots from Monday to Friday. The team deletes the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday snapshots. Can it still restore Friday's state of the volume? Answer: yes; you need to [retain only the most recent snapshot] (ebs-snapshot-deletion-keep-only-latest), because deletion removes [only the data that is referenced exclusively] by the deleted snapshot (ebs-snapshot-delete-removes-only-exclusive-data).

sections.heading: A restored volume can start in any zone but reads slowly at first

plan.problem: After a failure, the team restores the database volume from last night's snapshot. The volume appears in seconds, but the first queries are slow.
trace: **Pick any zone.** Snapshot data is [replicated across all Availability Zones in the Region], so you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones] (ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region); the new volume [begins as an exact replica of the volume] (ebs-volume-from-snapshot-exact-replica-same-az-attach).
**Pick the size.** The new size is [equal to or larger than] the snapshot's volume size (ebs-volume-from-snapshot-size-at-least-source).

**Blocks arrive when first read.** Each block is [downloaded from Amazon S3 to the new volume], and until then you see [increased I/O latency and decreased performance] (ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot).

**Or pay for full speed.** With fast snapshot restore a volume is [fully initialized at creation] (ebs-fsr-volume-fully-initialized-at-creation); with an initialization rate of [100 to 300 MiB/s] it is [fully performant in a predictable amount of time] (ebs-volume-initialization-rate-range).
plan.table: Ways to warm a restored volume (columns: Option | How | Cost): default | blocks load on first read, or you read every block yourself ([Use the dd or fio utilities], ebs-manual-initialization-read-all-blocks) | nothing extra; fast snapshot restore | enabled per snapshot in each zone (ebs-faq-fsr-enabled-per-az) | billed per minute with a [minimum of one hour] (ebs-fsr-billing-per-minute); initialization rate | set when you create the volume (ebs-faq-provisioned-rate-initialization) | per GiB [based on the full snapshot data size] (ebs-provisioned-rate-charged-on-snapshot-data).
plan.why: Why go through a snapshot? A volume stays in its zone, so a snapshot is how the same data reaches another zone: you [create a duplicate volume in that zone] (ebs-snapshot-restore-volume-other-az).
plan.exam_signal: "restore volumes at full performance immediately" or "boot many instances from a custom AMI without a warm-up" points to fast snapshot restore ([avoid the initial performance hit during initialization], ebs-faq-fsr-when-to-use); "move a volume to another Availability Zone" points to a snapshot and a new volume there (ebs-snapshot-restore-volume-other-az).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: fast snapshot restore credits. Each enabled snapshot has [one credit bucket per snapshot per Availability Zone] (ebs-fsr-credit-bucket-per-snapshot-az); a full bucket creates [up to 10 initialized volumes] at once (ebs-faq-fsr-up-to-10-volumes). An account can enable [up to 5 snapshots] per Region (ebs-fsr-5-snapshots-per-region). It [do not speed up snapshot creation time] (ebs-faq-fsr-not-faster-creation; rephrase so the display reads as part of the sentence). When you set a rate, EBS [uses the specified rate instead] of fast snapshot restore (ebs-provisioned-rate-overrides-fsr). At most 75 words.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: for a test copy, [Volume copies are created immediately] in the [same Availability Zone as the source volume] (ebs-volume-copy-instant-access, ebs-volume-copy-same-az). Reference only: root volume replacement on a running instance (ebs-replace-root-volume-running-instance), FSR limits and prices.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: restore the snapshot into any zone you need. The thing to watch is the slow first read of each block.
plan.stop_and_answer: A test team creates ten volumes from one snapshot every morning, and the first test run is always slow. Name two fixes. Answer: enable fast snapshot restore on that snapshot in that zone, so volumes are [fully initialized at creation] (ebs-fsr-volume-fully-initialized-at-creation), or set an initialization rate so they are [fully performant in a predictable amount of time] (ebs-volume-initialization-rate-range).

sections.heading: Copying or sharing a snapshot puts the backup in another Region or account

plan.problem: A snapshot survives the loss of a zone, but not the loss of a Region or of the account itself. For those, a copy must leave both.
trace: **Snapshots stay home.** [Snapshots are constrained to the Region] where you made them; to use one elsewhere, [copy the snapshot to that Region] (ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing).

**Copy across Regions.** You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another] (ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt); the first copy to a new Region is full, [a full (non-incremental) copy is created] (ebs-snapshot-copy-new-region-full-copy), and the copy is [charged for the data transferred across regions] (ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-charge).

**Share with accounts.** Snapshot permissions share [privately with individual AWS accounts] or publicly (ebs-snapshot-share-public-or-specific-accounts); [You can share only unencrypted snapshots publicly] (ebs-snapshot-only-unencrypted-public).

**Share the key too.** For an encrypted snapshot [you must also share the customer managed key] (ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too); [You can't share snapshots that are encrypted] with the AWS managed key (ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable).
plan.table: Can it be shared? (columns: Snapshot | With one account | Publicly): unencrypted | yes | yes, unless block public access is on (ebs-snapshot-bpa-blocks-public-sharing-in-region); encrypted, customer managed key | yes, with the key (ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too) | no (ebs-snapshot-only-unencrypted-public); encrypted, AWS managed key | no (ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable) | no.
plan.why: Why the key rule? The other account must decrypt the data, so you [apply cross-account permissions to a customer managed key] (ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too); an AWS managed key cannot be shared that way.
plan.exam_signal: "disaster recovery in another Region" for EBS data points to a cross-Region snapshot copy ([copy snapshots from one Region to another], ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt); "share an encrypted snapshot with another account" points to a customer managed key shared with that account (ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence each: block public access [is a Regional setting] (ebs-snapshot-bpa-regional-account-setting) and [does not prevent private snapshot sharing] (ebs-snapshot-bpa-not-private-or-ami-sharing); a time-based copy finishes [between 15 minutes and 48 hours] (ebs-time-based-copy-duration-range) to help [meet stringent disaster recovery requirements] (ebs-time-based-copy-for-rpo-rto). Reference only: tags and fast snapshot restore are not copied, re-copying a shared snapshot with your own key, DLM cross-account copy (subsection 13).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: copy the snapshot out of the Region and the account. The thing to watch is the key that encrypts it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team copies a snapshot from US East (N. Virginia) to US West (Oregon) every night. Why is the first night's transfer much larger than the next ones? Answer: the first copy to a new Region is [a full (non-incremental) copy is created] (ebs-snapshot-copy-new-region-full-copy; rephrase so the display reads as part of the sentence); later copies can be incremental when the guide's conditions are met ([the copy is an incremental copy]).

sections.heading: EBS encryption covers the volume, its snapshots and the path to the instance

plan.problem: A customer's security questionnaire asks whether every disk that holds their data is encrypted, the backups too. One unencrypted volume turns the answer into 'no'.
trace: **Choose the key.** EBS uses a KMS key: the AWS managed key [aws/ebs], [a unique AWS managed key in each Region] (ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-alias-per-region), unless you [create and use a customer managed key] (ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-unless-cmk).

**Encrypt on the host.** Encryption runs [on the servers that host Amazon EC2 instances], so it protects [data-at-rest and data-in-transit] between the instance and the volume (ebs-encryption-on-host-covers-in-transit), with [AES-256] (ebs-encryption-aes-256).

**It flows to copies.** [Snapshots of encrypted EBS volumes are automatically encrypted], and volumes [created from encrypted snapshots are automatically encrypted] (ebs-encryption-propagates-to-snapshots-and-volumes).
**No speed cost.** You get [the same IOPS performance on encrypted volumes] with [a minimal effect on latency] (ebs-encryption-same-iops-minimal-latency).

**Turn it on for new volumes.** Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting] (ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting) that encrypts new volumes and snapshot copies but [has no effect on existing EBS volumes] (ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only).
plan.table: Changing encryption later (columns: You want | Path): encrypt an existing volume | [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes]: snapshot, [create an encrypted copy of that snapshot], [create a new encrypted volume] (ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot); remove encryption | not possible: [You cannot remove encryption] (ebs-encryption-cannot-be-removed); change the KMS key | copy the snapshot with a new key ([during a snapshot copy operation], ebs-encryption-key-fixed-change-on-copy); encrypt every new volume | encryption by default, in each Region ([single setting per region], ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region).
plan.why: Why encrypt on the host? The data is encrypted before it leaves the server, so the path to the volume is covered too ([data-at-rest and data-in-transit], ebs-encryption-on-host-covers-in-transit). The security pillar says to [Encrypt private data at rest] (ebs-wa-sec08-encrypt-at-rest).
plan.exam_signal: "ensure that all new EBS volumes are encrypted" points to encryption by default in each Region ([single setting per region], ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region); "encrypt an existing unencrypted volume" points to a snapshot, an encrypted copy and a new volume (ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug prompt: before an audit, an administrator turns on EBS encryption by default in US East (N. Virginia) and reports that every volume of the account is now encrypted. What is wrong? Reveal: the setting [has no effect on existing EBS volumes] (ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only) and is [a Region-specific setting] (ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting); old volumes need a snapshot, an encrypted copy and a new volume (ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), and every other Region needs the setting too. About 60 words with the reveal.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: you can launch from an unencrypted AMI and [encrypt some or all of the volumes] (ebs-faq-encrypted-from-unencrypted-ami); users need permissions on the key ([You must grant users permission to call], ebs-encryption-users-need-kms-permissions). Reference only: NVMe instance store encryption (instance-store-nvme-encryption-xts-aes-256), an unusable key (kms-unusable-key-ebs-attach-fails), mixed volumes on one instance.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: encrypt with a KMS key, and snapshots inherit it. The thing to watch is old volumes: they need an encrypted copy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company turned on encryption by default last month. A developer restores a volume from an old unencrypted snapshot. Is the new volume encrypted? Answer: yes; with encryption by default on, [encryption is mandatory for volumes restored] from unencrypted snapshots (ebs-encrypted-snapshot-restore-default-key).

sections.heading: Data Lifecycle Manager and AWS Backup take snapshots on a schedule

plan.problem: A backup that a person must remember is a backup that someone forgets. Snapshots need a schedule, a retention rule and a place to keep old ones cheaply.
trace: **Write a policy.** Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots] and EBS-backed AMIs [at no additional cost] (ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis).
**Target by tag.** A custom policy can [use resource tags to identify the resources] it backs up (ebs-dlm-custom-policies-target-by-tags).

**Schedule and keep.** A schedule runs on a [daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly schedule] and keeps snapshots by [either their total count or their age] (ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type).

**Copy away.** A schedule can copy snapshots to [up to three additional Regions or Outposts] (ebs-dlm-cross-region-copy-three-regions) or to [specific Regions in an isolated account] (ebs-dlm-cross-account-copy-isolated-account).
**Archive the old ones.** The archive tier gives [up to 75 percent lower snapshot storage costs] for snapshots kept [90 days or longer] (ebs-archive-75-percent-lower-cost).
plan.table: Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup (columns: Question | Data Lifecycle Manager | AWS Backup): protects | EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs (ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis) | many services: it [supports many AWS services] (ebs-aws-backup-central-policy-across-accounts); one policy reaches | the volumes it targets in one Region, plus copies | [apply it across accounts and Regions]; extra protection | a copy in an isolated account (ebs-dlm-cross-account-copy-isolated-account) | [Vault Lock enforces immutability] (ebs-aws-backup-air-gapped-vault-lock); price of the tool | [at no additional cost] | not stated here (write no price).
plan.why: Why automate? AWS [does not automatically back up the data] (ebs-no-automatic-backup-customer-creates-snapshots), and services such as EBS [have built in capabilities to create backups] that AWS Backup can [centralize and automate data protection across AWS services] (ebs-wa-rel09-backup-capabilities).
plan.exam_signal: "automate the creation, retention and deletion of EBS snapshots" points to Data Lifecycle Manager ([creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots], ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis); "one backup policy across accounts and services" points to AWS Backup ([apply it across accounts and Regions], ebs-aws-backup-central-policy-across-accounts).
plan.startup_example: Startup example callout, story only, at most 60 words with the label, numbers only from uses_numbers (disk_full_incident: newest backup 9 days old; snapshot_keep_days 30): 'When the volume filled up, Callvale's newest backup was 9 days old, because Ben made backups by hand. Now one Data Lifecycle Manager policy takes a snapshot of the database volume every day and keeps it for 30 days.' The story states no AWS rule; the trace above carries the facts.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence each: archived snapshots have a [minimum archive period is 90 days] (ebs-archive-min-period-90-days) and a restore can take [up to 72 hours] (ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours), so AWS suggests archiving [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots] (ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily); default policies back up volumes [that do not have recent backups] (ebs-dlm-default-policies-unbacked-resources); pre and post scripts [freeze and flush I/O] for application-consistent snapshots (ebs-dlm-app-consistent-pre-post-scripts). Reference only: schedule counts, retention ranges, the four-hour window, the 24-hour minimum age.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a policy takes and deletes snapshots for you. The thing to watch is scope across services and accounts.

sections.heading: Recycle Bin and snapshot lock stop snapshots from being deleted too early

plan.problem: An engineer deletes the wrong snapshot, or an attacker deletes all of them. A backup schedule does not help once the backups are gone.
trace: **Catch deletions.** Recycle Bin restores deleted [EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and EBS-backed AMIs], kept [for a time period that you specify] (ebs-recycle-bin-recovers-volumes-snapshots-amis).

**Write a rule in each Region.** To get protection [you must create retention rules] [in the AWS Regions in which you want] it (ebs-recycle-bin-needs-regional-retention-rules); a matching deleted snapshot is [retained in the Recycle Bin] (ebs-snapshot-delete-retained-by-recycle-bin-rule).
**Restore in time.** You restore [at any time before its retention period expires]; after that the resource is [no longer available for recovery] (ebs-recycle-bin-expired-permanently-deleted).

**Lock what must stay.** While a snapshot is locked, [it can't be deleted by any user] [regardless of their IAM permissions] (ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete); in compliance mode, after the cooling-off period, [you can't unlock the snapshot] (ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode).
plan.table: Two guards (columns: Question | Recycle Bin | Snapshot lock): protects | volumes, snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs (ebs-recycle-bin-recovers-volumes-snapshots-amis) | snapshots (ebs-snapshot-lock-modes); when it acts | after a delete: the resource waits in the bin | before a delete: the delete is refused (ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete); how you choose what | tag-level or Region-level rules (ebs-recycle-bin-tag-and-region-level-rules) | [compliance mode or governance mode] (ebs-snapshot-lock-modes); cost | [billed at the same rate as regular snapshots] (ebs-recycle-bin-billed-same-rate) | lock and unlock [at no additional cost] (ebs-snapshot-lock-no-additional-cost).
plan.why: Why two tools? Recycle Bin undoes a mistake after it happens; a lock stops the delete before it happens, also for an administrator ([regardless of their IAM permissions], ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete).
plan.exam_signal: "recover accidentally deleted EBS snapshots" points to Recycle Bin ([EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and EBS-backed AMIs], ebs-recycle-bin-recovers-volumes-snapshots-amis); "WORM" or "no user, administrators included, can delete the backups" points to snapshot lock in compliance mode ([you can't unlock the snapshot], ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode) or AWS Backup Vault Lock ([Vault Lock enforces immutability], ebs-aws-backup-air-gapped-vault-lock).

Reference only: the retention range, rule locks and the unlock delay, lock durations and the cooling-off range. Recycle Bin protects volumes since 2025-11-20 (Changed recently in 1-fast.md).

Can the team restore it from Recycle Bin? Answer: no; protection exists [in the AWS Regions in which you want] it, where [you must create retention rules] (ebs-recycle-bin-needs-regional-retention-rules).

traps.belief: An EBS volume can be attached to an instance in any Availability Zone of its Region.
traps.truth: The volume and the instance must be in the same Availability Zone; to use the data in another zone, take a snapshot and create a new volume there.

traps.belief: Instance store is fast and free, so it is a good place for data that the company must keep, such as a database.
traps.truth: Instance store is for temporary data: its data is lost when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or when the disk fails; keep data that matters on EBS or in Amazon S3.

traps.belief: EBS volumes persist, so the root volume stays when the instance is terminated.
traps.truth: By default the root volume created at launch is deleted on termination; other volumes created at launch are kept. The DeleteOnTermination flag changes this.

traps.belief: st1 or sc1 is a cheaper choice for a database or a boot volume.
traps.truth: HDD volumes perform poorly for small, random I/O such as a database, and they cannot be boot volumes.

traps.belief: To get more IOPS from a General Purpose SSD volume, you must make it bigger.
traps.truth: That is true for gp2, whose IOPS grow with size; gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size.

traps.belief: Every production database needs Provisioned IOPS (io2) volumes.
traps.truth: gp3 fits medium-sized single-instance databases at lower cost; AWS recommends io2 Block Express when a workload needs more durability, more consistent latency, or more IOPS and throughput than gp3 can provide.

traps.belief: Elastic Volumes can make an over-provisioned volume smaller.
traps.truth: You cannot decrease the size of a volume; create a smaller volume and copy the data to it.

traps.belief: With Multi-Attach, many instances in several Availability Zones can share one volume like a shared file system, with an ordinary file system on it.
traps.truth: Multi-Attach works for io1 and io2 volumes and instances in one Availability Zone, and needs a clustered file system or an application that coordinates writes; Amazon EFS shares files across Availability Zones.

traps.belief: Snapshots are incremental, so deleting an older snapshot breaks the newer ones.
traps.truth: Deleting a snapshot removes only the data that no other snapshot references; the most recent snapshot alone restores the volume.

traps.belief: A volume restored from a snapshot gives its full performance as soon as it is created.
traps.truth: Its blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 when first read, so I/O is slower until it is initialized; fast snapshot restore or an initialization rate avoids the wait.

traps.belief: Any encrypted snapshot can be shared with another AWS account.
traps.truth: A snapshot encrypted with the AWS managed key cannot be shared; encrypt it with a customer managed key and share that key too.

traps.belief: You can turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted volume, or encryption by default encrypts the volumes you already have.
traps.truth: You cannot encrypt an existing volume directly: snapshot it, make an encrypted copy and create a new volume; encryption by default has no effect on existing volumes.

traps.belief: EBS replicates every volume, so AWS already keeps a backup of the data.
traps.truth: Replication inside the Availability Zone protects against a hardware failure, not against deletion or the loss of the zone; AWS does not back up the data, and snapshots are the customer's job.

traps.belief: To recover an EBS volume after the loss of its Availability Zone, the snapshot must first be copied to another Region.
traps.truth: Snapshot data is replicated across all Availability Zones of its Region, so a volume can be restored in any other zone of the same Region; a copy to a second Region is needed only for the loss of the Region.
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: To give an EBS volume more space, you must move its data to a new, larger volume.
traps.truth: Elastic Volumes increases the size of the volume in place, without detaching the volume or restarting the instance; then you extend the partition and the file system.
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: Any EBS volume type, gp3 included, can be attached to several instances with Multi-Attach.
traps.truth: Multi-Attach is supported only on Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes (io1 and io2).
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: More provisioned IOPS or more volumes always raise the EBS performance of an instance.
traps.truth: EBS performance of an instance is bounded by the instance type's limits or by its volumes, whichever is smaller; when the instance is the limit, only a larger instance type helps.
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: EBS encryption by default is one account setting that covers every Region.
traps.truth: Encryption by default is a Region-specific setting; turn it on in each Region where volumes are created.
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: io2 Block Express volumes are so durable that their data needs no snapshots.
traps.truth: Volume durability, snapshots and copies in other Availability Zones protect against different types of failures; durability does not bring back deleted data, and AWS does not back up the volume for you.
traps.note: added by questions-22-2 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: A Recycle Bin retention rule stops users from deleting a snapshot.
traps.truth: Recycle Bin acts after a delete: it keeps a deleted snapshot for recovery until the retention period expires. To stop the delete itself, lock the snapshot.
traps.note: added by questions-22-2 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: A snapshot locked in governance mode is safe from every user, administrators included.
traps.truth: In governance mode, users with the right IAM permissions can unlock the snapshot; in compliance mode, after the cooling-off period, the snapshot cannot be unlocked.
traps.note: added by questions-22-2 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: The snapshot archive tier lowers the cost of any snapshot, daily ones included.
traps.truth: AWS recommends the archive tier for monthly, quarterly or yearly snapshots; an archived snapshot becomes a full snapshot, so archiving the daily incremental snapshots of a volume can cost more.
traps.note: added by questions-22-2 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

traps.belief: EBS snapshots sit in an Amazon S3 bucket that you can read, copy or move with the Amazon S3 API.
traps.truth: Snapshots are stored in S3 buckets that you cannot access directly; you manage them through the Amazon EC2 console and API.
traps.note: added by questions-22-1 for distractor tagging (Q205); used in questions only, not planned as a callout

decision_record.context: The trigger of data/startup.json chapter 22, at most 80 words, stage 1, month 6: on a Tuesday at 09:40 the only volume of the instance fills up; it holds the operating system, the database and temporary audio files; the database stops for 3 hours; the newest backup is 9 days old (disk_full_incident). Callvale's own targets: an RPO of 24 hours and an RTO of 8 hours (stage1_rpo_hours, stage1_rto_hours).
decision_record.requirement: The database must lose at most 24 hours of data and must recover within 8 hours, and a full disk must not stop it again, with the solution that is fastest to implement (qualifier of the JSON: fastest to implement).
options: a separate data volume with daily snapshots (chosen)
move the database to a managed service now
decision_record.decision: A separate gp3 data volume for the database, with daily snapshots kept for 30 days (data/startup.json choice), encrypted, and with the snapshots taken by a Data Lifecycle Manager policy (adds).
reasons_with_facts: Option 1 keeps the operating system, the database and the temporary files on one volume, so temporary files can fill it again; the EC2 best practices keep [separate Amazon EBS volumes for the operating system] and for data (ec2-bp-separate-ebs-for-os-and-data). A larger volume is also no backup: AWS [does not automatically back up the data] (ebs-no-automatic-backup-customer-creates-snapshots).
Option 3 solves more (chapter 26 does it at month 8) but is not the fastest to implement; keep this reason as story, with no AWS claim.

Option 2: the data volume can start at the size the database needs, with performance set [independently of volume size] (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), and can grow [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance] (ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach). The policy automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots] (ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis) and keeps snapshots by [either their total count or their age] (ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type), so the newest backup is at most a day old (RPO 24 hours). A snapshot can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones] of the Region (ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region), which fits the RTO of 8 hours even though the restored volume is slower until initialized (ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot). New volumes are encrypted by default ([single setting per region], ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region); the old root volume gets an encrypted copy through a snapshot (ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot).
decision_record.tradeoff: The database still depends on one instance in one Availability Zone. Chapter 26 removes that risk two months later (data/startup.json tradeoff, word for word).
decision_record.later: One sentence at most: at stage 2 the conversion workers keep the temporary files of one call on instance store volumes (data/startup.json later); chapter 24 moves the backups to AWS Backup at stage 3. No new option in the record.
