question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair A (twin q06)
question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company runs a workload on one EC2 instance with one EBS data volume and wants the volume type that meets the need MOST cost-effectively. Changed phrase: 'The workload is a relational database with small, random reads and writes that needs about 10,000 IOPS.' Key: (A) gp3 ([balance between cost and performance], ebs-faq-gp3-suited-workloads; ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size). Options identical in q06: (A) General Purpose SSD (gp3); (B) Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) (trap ebs-trap-io2-for-every-database; violates-qualifier; why links ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when); (C) Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) (trap ebs-trap-hdd-for-database-or-boot; why links ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io); (D) Cold HDD (sc1) (trap ebs-trap-hdd-for-database-or-boot). The 10,000 IOPS sits below the old and the new gp3 maximum, so the gp3 change of 2025-09-26 decides nothing: never cite ebs-gp3-max-iops-80000 in the key. Bullets also 4.1.S10.

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair B (twin q09)
question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company runs a processing application on EC2 instances; each instance writes many temporary files while it works on a job; which storage meets these requirements? Changed phrase: 'The files are scratch data that the application can re-create from Amazon S3, and the job needs the lowest possible storage latency.' Key: (A) instance store volumes ([buffers, caches, scratch data], instance-store-ideal-for-temporary-data; [high random I/O performance with very low latency], instance-store-ssd-high-random-io). Options identical in q09: (A) instance store volumes on an instance type that provides them; (B) an EBS gp3 volume on each instance (violates-qualifier in q02: network latency and storage cost for data that can be re-created; why links ebs-faq-average-latency); (C) one Amazon EFS file system mounted on all instances (misconception: shared file storage is not needed; why links ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access); (D) an EBS sc1 volume on each instance (misconception: HDD for small random I/O, trap ebs-trap-hdd-for-database-or-boot). Bullets also 3.1.K3, 2.2.K11.

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair C (twin q12)
question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company runs a database on one EC2 instance with an EBS data volume; the company accepts losing up to one day of data. Changed phrase: 'The company must be able to recover the database if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable.' Key: (A) take a daily EBS snapshot and, after a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the Region ([restore volumes in any Availability Zones], ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region). Options identical in q12: (A) as above; (B) take a daily EBS snapshot and copy it to a second Region, then restore it there after a failure (violates-qualifier in q03: transfer and storage in a second Region, ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-charge); (C) after a failure, attach the existing volume to a new instance in another Availability Zone (trap ebs-trap-volume-attaches-across-azs; why links ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance); (D) change the volume to io2 Block Express for higher durability (misconception; why links ebs-faq-io2-still-snapshot-and-replicate). Qualifier MOST cost-effective. Bullets also 2.2.K11.

A database runs on a 100 GiB gp2 volume and needs 8,000 IOPS; the data will stay near 100 GiB; minimal downtime; MOST cost-effective. Key: change the volume to gp3 with Elastic Volumes and provision 8,000 IOPS (ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size, ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach, ebs-gp3-20-percent-lower-price). Distractors: grow the gp2 volume until its baseline reaches 8,000 IOPS (trap ebs-trap-grow-gp-volume-for-iops; why links ebs-gp2-iops-per-gib); change to io2 Block Express with 8,000 IOPS (violates-qualifier; ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when); build a RAID 0 array of gp2 volumes (violates-qualifier: more volumes and more work; ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume). 8,000 IOPS is below the old and new gp3 maximum: never cite the volatile maximum in the key. Bullets also 3.1.S1, 4.1.S10.

A mission-critical database on one Nitro-based instance needs consistent sub-millisecond latency and the highest volume durability that EBS offers. Which volume type? Key: io2 Block Express ([consistent sub-millisecond latency], ebs-io2-use-cases; [99.999 percent volume durability], ebs-io2-durability-afr). Distractors: gp3 with provisioned IOPS (violates-requirement: [single-digit millisecond latency], ebs-gp3-latency); st1 for its throughput (trap ebs-trap-hdd-for-database-or-boot); a RAID 0 array of gp3 volumes (misconception: striping adds IOPS, not durability or lower latency; ebs-raid0-one-volume-loss-loses-array). The deciding facts are latency and durability, which did not change; do not let an IOPS maximum decide. Bullets also 3.1.S1, 2.2.K11.

question_slots.twin: second of strict twin pair A (twin_of q01)
question_slots.note: Same shared stem and the same four options as q01. Changed phrase: 'The workload is a log processing job that reads large files sequentially many times a day and must finish each scan quickly.' Key: (C) st1 ([Big data, data warehouses, log processing], ebs-st1-use-cases; [frequently accessed, throughput-intensive workloads], ebs-st1-low-cost-frequent-throughput). Wrong: (A) gp3 (violates-qualifier: SSD price for sequential throughput; ebs-ssd-transactional-hdd-throughput-categories); (B) io2 Block Express (violates-qualifier; trap ebs-trap-io2-for-every-database); (D) sc1 (trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-cheapest-wins: lowest cost per GB, but for rarely scanned data, ebs-st1-vs-sc1-scan-choice). The twin line of each question quotes the other's changed phrase. Bullets also 3.1.S1.

A company has one unencrypted EBS data volume and must encrypt its data at rest; it must also ensure that every new volume in the Region is encrypted. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.) Keys: create a snapshot, copy it with encryption, create a new volume from the encrypted copy and swap it in (ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot); turn on EBS encryption by default in the Region (ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region). Distractors (five options): modify the existing volume with Elastic Volumes to turn on encryption (trap ebs-trap-encrypt-volume-in-place; why links kms-ebs-encryption-status-fixed-at-create); turn on encryption by default and wait for it to encrypt the existing volume (trap ebs-trap-encrypt-volume-in-place; why links ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only); move the data to an instance store volume, which is encrypted (misconception: temporary storage; instance-store-faq-only-temporary-data).

qualifier 'none' (difficulty 1). Instances are launched with an EBS root volume and default settings. After an instance is terminated, the company must retain the data of its root volume for an audit. What should the company change for future launches? Key: set DeleteOnTermination to false for the root volume at launch ([DeleteOnTermination to false], ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true; ebs-faq-root-delete-on-termination-no). Distractors: nothing, because EBS volumes persist after termination (trap ebs-trap-terminate-keeps-root-volume); copy the root volume data to an instance store volume before termination (misconception; instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop); set DeleteOnTermination to true (misconception: that deletes the volume). State the stem so that exactly one option is right.

question_slots.twin: second of strict twin pair B (twin_of q02)
question_slots.note: Same shared stem and the same four options as q02. Changed phrase: 'The files must still be there after the instances are stopped and started again for maintenance every weekend.' Key: (B) an EBS gp3 volume on each instance ([remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle], ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start). Wrong: (A) instance store (trap ebs-trap-instance-store-for-durable-data, or ec2-trap-stop-keeps-instance-store; why links instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop); (C) Amazon EFS (violates-qualifier: shared storage the files do not need; give the stem a qualifier such as MOST cost-effective so that C is clearly wrong); (D) sc1 (misconception: HDD for small random I/O, ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io). Bullets also 2.2.K11.

A company has taken a daily snapshot of one volume for a year; storage cost is high; it needs point-in-time restores for the last 7 days only. MOST cost-effective? Key: keep the last 7 daily snapshots and delete the older ones, for example with an age-based Data Lifecycle Manager retention rule (ebs-snapshot-delete-removes-only-exclusive-data, ebs-snapshot-deletion-keep-only-latest, ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type). Distractors: keep every snapshot, because deleting an older incremental snapshot breaks the newer ones (trap ebs-trap-delete-old-snapshot-breaks-restore); move all daily snapshots to the archive tier (misconception: AWS recommends archive for monthly or yearly snapshots, ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily); delete the volume, because its snapshots then cost less (misconception; ebs-snapshot-and-volume-delete-independent). Bullets also 1.3.S5, 4.1.S10.

A company encrypts its EBS snapshots with the AWS managed key aws/ebs and must give a separate, isolated backup account copies of them. Most secure way? Key: copy the snapshots with a customer managed key, give the backup account permissions on that key, and share the copies with that account only (ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable, ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too, ebs-encryption-key-fixed-change-on-copy). Distractors: share the snapshots that use aws/ebs directly (trap ebs-trap-share-snapshot-with-aws-managed-key); make the snapshots public so the backup account can copy them (impossible-feature: encrypted snapshots cannot be public, ebs-snapshot-only-unencrypted-public; also violates most secure); edit the key policy of aws/ebs to allow the backup account (trap kms-trap-aws-managed-key-controllable). Bullets also 1.3.S2.

question_slots.twin: second of strict twin pair C (twin_of q03)
question_slots.note: Same shared stem and the same four options as q03. Changed phrase: 'The company must be able to recover the database if the whole Region becomes unavailable.' Key: (B) daily snapshot copied to a second Region and restored there ([copy snapshots from one Region to another], ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt; [Snapshots are constrained to the Region], ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing). Wrong: (A) restore in another zone of the same Region (violates-requirement: the Region is down; trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-multi-az-covers-region); (C) attach the volume in another zone (trap ebs-trap-volume-attaches-across-azs); (D) io2 durability (misconception, ebs-faq-io2-still-snapshot-and-replicate). Bullets also 2.2.S5.

qualifier 'none' (difficulty 1); the requirement is 'without downtime'. A data volume on a running instance is almost full; the application cannot stop. What should the team do? Key: increase the volume size with Elastic Volumes, then extend the partition and file system (ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach, ebs-extend-partition-after-size-increase). Distractors: stop the instance, detach the volume and attach a larger new one (violates-requirement: downtime); create a snapshot and restore it to a larger volume (violates-requirement: a swap and slow first reads, ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot); add an instance store volume to the running instance (impossible-feature: instance store is added [only when you launch it], instance-store-attach-only-at-launch). Bullets also 4.1.S2.

A 2 TiB gp3 data volume holds 200 GiB of data that grows slowly; the company wants to cut the storage cost. MOST cost-effective? Key: create a smaller gp3 volume, copy the data with an application-level tool, switch the application to it and delete the old volume ([You can't decrease the volume size], [create a smaller volume], ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease; ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month). Wrong path in the think-aloud: step 3 predicts 'shrink the volume with Elastic Volumes'; step 5: 'My first idea breaks because a volume cannot be made smaller.' Distractors: modify the volume to 300 GiB with Elastic Volumes (trap ebs-trap-shrink-volume); take a snapshot and restore it into a 300 GiB volume (impossible-feature: the size must be [equal to or larger than] the snapshot's volume size, ebs-volume-from-snapshot-size-at-least-source); change the volume type to sc1 (violates-requirement for a database volume, trap ebs-trap-hdd-for-database-or-boot). At most one impossible-feature distractor. Bullets also 4.1.S2.

A clustered application runs on two Nitro-based Linux instances in one Availability Zone; both must read and write the same block storage so that either node can take over at once. Which combination of steps? (Select TWO.) Keys: create an io2 Block Express volume with Multi-Attach and attach it to both instances (ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az, ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only); use a clustered file system or cluster software that coordinates writes, for example with NVMe reservations (ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system, ebs-faq-multi-attach-application-requirements). Distractors (five options): format the volume with XFS and mount it on both instances (trap ebs-trap-multi-attach-as-shared-file-system); create a gp3 volume with Multi-Attach (impossible-feature, ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only); move one instance to a second Availability Zone and attach the same volume there (trap ebs-trap-multi-attach-as-shared-file-system; ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az). Bullets also 3.1.S1.

Web servers in three Availability Zones must read and write the same set of files. LEAST operational overhead? Key: one Amazon EFS file system mounted on all servers ([within and across multiple Availability Zones], ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing; ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access). Distractors: one io2 volume with Multi-Attach for all servers (trap ebs-trap-multi-attach-as-shared-file-system); a gp3 volume on each server with a copy job between them (violates-qualifier); instance store volumes with a copy job (misconception; instance-store-faq-only-temporary-data). Bullets also 4.1.K4, 4.1.K11, 3.1.K3.

A database on one instance uses two io2 Block Express volumes; together they are provisioned well above the IOPS the database gets; however, neither volume reports throttling of its own. The team must raise database I/O. Key: move to a larger Nitro-based instance type with a higher EBS limit (ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller; ebs-io2-nitro-iops-limit). Distractors: provision more IOPS on each volume (misconception: the instance is the limit, [whichever is smaller]); add a third volume in a RAID 0 array (misconception: the same instance limit; ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume); change both volumes to gp3 (misconception; ebs-gp3-latency). State the instance limit in the stem as scenario data so that exactly one option is right. Bullets also 3.1.S2.

Every morning a company creates many volumes from one snapshot for a test fleet in one Availability Zone; the volumes must deliver full performance as soon as they are created. Key: enable fast snapshot restore on that snapshot in that Availability Zone ([fully initialized at creation], ebs-fsr-volume-fully-initialized-at-creation; ebs-faq-fsr-enabled-per-az). Distractors: nothing, restored volumes are fast at once (trap ebs-trap-restored-volume-full-speed); change the volumes to io2 Block Express (misconception: the blocks still come from Amazon S3, ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot); copy the snapshot to the same Region every morning (misconception: a copy does not inherit fast snapshot restore, ebs-snapshot-copy-fsr-not-inherited). Bullets also 2.2.S5.

A company creates EBS volumes in two Regions and must make sure that every new volume is encrypted at rest. LEAST operational overhead? Key: turn on EBS encryption by default in each of the two Regions (ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting, ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region). Distractors: turn it on once in one Region, because the setting applies to the whole account (misconception: [a Region-specific setting]); write a script that checks new volumes each hour and encrypts the unencrypted ones in place (misconception and violates-qualifier: no in-place encryption, ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot); use instance store volumes, which are always encrypted (misconception: temporary data; instance-store-faq-only-temporary-data). Avoid an SCP or AWS Config option: either could be argued right.

A company must back up the EBS volumes of an application every day, keep each backup 30 days, and be able to recover a snapshot that an operator deletes by mistake, with the LEAST operational overhead. (Select TWO.) Keys: a Data Lifecycle Manager policy with a daily schedule and age-based retention (ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis, ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type); a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots in that Region (ebs-recycle-bin-recovers-volumes-snapshots-amis, ebs-recycle-bin-needs-regional-retention-rules). Distractors (five options): rely on EBS replication, which already keeps copies (trap ebs-trap-aws-backs-up-ebs); a cron job on each instance that calls the AWS CLI (violates-qualifier); change the volumes to io2 Block Express for durability (misconception; ebs-faq-io2-still-snapshot-and-replicate). Bullets also 1.3.S5.

A company keeps one EBS snapshot a month for seven years for compliance; the snapshots are accessed infrequently, and a restore within three days is acceptable. MOST cost-effective? Key: move the monthly snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier ([up to 75 percent lower snapshot storage costs], ebs-archive-75-percent-lower-cost; [up to 72 hours], ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours; ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily). Distractors: keep them in the standard tier (violates-qualifier); copy the snapshots into an S3 bucket with S3 Glacier Deep Archive through the S3 API (impossible-feature: snapshots are reached [only available through the Amazon EC2 API], ebs-faq-snapshots-not-via-s3-api); delete all but the newest snapshot (violates-requirement: seven years of monthly states). Bullets also 2.2.S5.

An auditor requires that a set of EBS snapshots be immutable for one year: no user, administrators included, may delete them. Key: lock the snapshots in compliance mode for one year ([it can't be deleted by any user], [regardless of their IAM permissions], ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete; [you can't unlock the snapshot], ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode). Distractors: lock them in governance mode (misconception: [users with appropriate IAM permissions can unlock], ebs-snapshot-lock-governance-mode); a Recycle Bin retention rule of 365 days (misconception: it keeps deleted snapshots but does not stop the delete); an IAM policy that denies ec2:DeleteSnapshot to all users (misconception: an administrator can change the policy). Do not offer AWS Backup Vault Lock as an option: it would also be right. Bullets also 1.3.S5.

tasks.title: Read your encryption default and find instance store
tasks.kills: "Every new EBS volume is encrypted automatically."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0. (1) aws ec2 get-ebs-encryption-by-default: expect true or false for this Region; it is [a Region-specific setting] (ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting). (2) aws ec2 get-ebs-default-kms-key-id: expect the key that encryption uses, the alias [aws/ebs] unless you chose another (ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-alias-per-region). (3) aws ec2 get-snapshot-block-public-access-state: expect the state of block public access for snapshots in this Region ([is a Regional setting], ebs-snapshot-bpa-regional-account-setting). (4) aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m5.large m5d.large with a --query on InstanceType, InstanceStorageSupported and InstanceStorageInfo.TotalSizeInGB, --output table: expect that only the type with the letter d has instance store ([Instance store volumes], ec2-instance-type-option-letters; instance-store-size-varies-by-type). Creates nothing. The writer confirms each operation and the query fields with tasks check-cli --reference; drop step 3 if the reference does not list it.

tasks.title: Grow and retune a gp3 volume then try to shrink it
tasks.kills: "Elastic Volumes can make an over-provisioned volume smaller."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 12 minutes, no instance needed. Cost line: gp3 storage at [$0.08 per GB-month] (ebs-gp3-storage-price-example) and IOPS above the baseline at [$0.005 per provisioned IOPS-month] (ebs-gp3-iops-price-example), billed in [per-second increments, with a 60-second minimum] (ebs-billing-per-second-60-second-minimum): a few cents at most for the minutes the volumes exist; state an amount only as a display of a price fact (T109), and the cost_if_forgotten line as the monthly rates. Steps: capture the first Availability Zone name (aws ec2 describe-availability-zones, query AvailabilityZones[0].ZoneName, capture AZ); create-volume --availability-zone $AZ --size 4 --volume-type gp3 --encrypted with --tag-specifications ResourceType=volume and tags book=saa and task=ebs-t02 (capture VOL_ID); aws ec2 wait volume-available; modify-volume --volume-id $VOL_ID --size 8 --iops 4000 (8 GiB allows 4,000 IOPS at [500 IOPS per GiB], ebs-gp3-max-iops-80000); describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids $VOL_ID: expect the state modifying or optimizing (ebs-modification-size-effective-at-optimizing). Break it: predict 'Can you shrink the volume back to 4 GiB?'; modify-volume --volume-id $VOL_ID --size 4: expect an error; explain [You can't decrease the volume size] (ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease). Fix: create a new 4 GiB gp3 volume with the same tags (capture SMALL_ID) and say that the data would move with a copy tool on an instance ([create a smaller volume], same fact). Cleanup in reverse order: delete-volume $SMALL_ID, delete-volume $VOL_ID. Verify: aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=tag:task,Values=ebs-t02 with --query Volumes[].VolumeId: expect an empty list after cleanup. Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'. speak.prompt: If that instance fails tomorrow, what do we lose, and how long are we offline?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'volume' as 'the disk the database writes to' and 'snapshot' as 'a nightly copy kept outside the building' the first time. Short answer: if only the server fails, we lose nothing on the database disk; it lives apart from the server and moves to a new one. If the disk or the whole data center zone fails, we restore last night's copy: we lose up to one day of data and need a few hours. How it works: the disk is copied inside one zone against hardware faults; the nightly copy is stored outside that zone and can rebuild the disk anywhere in the Region. Watch: everything still runs in one zone until we move the database to a managed service; and the first hour after a restore is slower. In your case: 'Can our customers accept losing one day of analysis in the worst case?' Must not say: 'AWS backs up the disk for us'; 'we lose nothing, ever'; 'the restored disk is fast at once'. Numbers as words: one day, eight hours (story values).

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: The AWS page says io2 is for databases. Should we pay for io2, or is gp3 enough for our Postgres?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both are SSD volumes that run databases well. Short answer: start on gp3; move to io2 Block Express only when a number demands it. How it works: gp3 lets you buy IOPS without buying space; io2 Block Express adds sub-millisecond latency and higher durability for a higher price. Watch: the instance type also limits disk speed, so a faster volume can change nothing. In your case: 'What latency and how many IOPS does your database need at the peak today?' Must not say: 'every production database needs io2'; 'gp3 is only for test systems'; 'io2 means you need no backups'. Spoken numbers from the say forms if used: ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent volume durability.

speak.prompt: Can all our web servers share one EBS volume with Multi-Attach, instead of paying for a file system?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both let several servers reach the same data, but in different ways. Short answer: no, use Amazon EFS for shared files; Multi-Attach is for cluster software in one zone. How it works: Multi-Attach gives one io2 volume to up to sixteen servers in one zone, and the cluster software must stop two servers from writing the same block; EFS is a file system that servers in every zone mount. Watch: a normal file system on a Multi-Attach volume can corrupt data. In your case: 'Do your web servers run in more than one Availability Zone?' Must not say: 'Multi-Attach works across zones'; 'any file system is safe on a Multi-Attach volume'; 'gp3 supports Multi-Attach'.

speak.prompt: Our auditor found unencrypted volumes from last year. How do we encrypt them, and how do we stop this from happening again?
speak.note: Short answer: you cannot switch on encryption for an old volume; you make an encrypted copy and move to it, and you turn on encryption by default in every Region you use. How it works: take a snapshot, copy it with encryption, create a new volume from the copy and swap it in during a short window; snapshots of encrypted volumes stay encrypted. Watch: the default setting is per Region and does nothing for existing volumes. In your case: 'Which Regions does your team create volumes in?' Must not say: 'turning on encryption by default fixes the old volumes'; 'encryption slows the database down'; 'encrypt the volume in place with Elastic Volumes'.

diagrams.title: A write, a copy in the zone and a snapshot
diagrams.claim: A volume serves its own Availability Zone, and its snapshots in Amazon S3 can rebuild it anywhere in the Region.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with three participants: an EC2 instance, an EBS volume and Amazon S3. The instance writes blocks to the volume in its zone, EBS copies the volume inside that zone, a snapshot sends the changed blocks to Amazon S3, and a new volume is restored from it in another zone.

The volume and the instance must be in the same Availability Zone.
The volume is automatically replicated within its Availability Zone.
A snapshot copies the blocks on the volume that have changed to Amazon S3.
The snapshot is stored redundantly in multiple Availability Zones.
From the snapshot, you can restore volumes in any Availability Zones of the Region.
